en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Cūḷaganthavaṃsa Pāḷi 1.
The Section on the Three Piṭakas
Having paid homage to the Fully Awakened One, the most excellent of the supreme lineage,
and having bowed to the Dhamma born of the Buddha and also to the stainless Saṅgha;
and relying upon the lineage of the textual tradition, I shall now relate that lineage of the texts.
Listen well, O virtuous ones, to this collection of the Tipiṭaka, which begins with the removal of doubts and includes the Sādhunaṃ Jaṅghadāsaka;
it comprises the entire word of the Buddha and liberation along with its causes.
It is of one kind alone, and threefold by way of the Piṭakas;
and all that together is fivefold according to the Nikāyas,
ninefold according to the Aṅgas, and [innumerable] when reckoned by the number of Dhamma-aggregates.
"The eighty-four thousand divisions of the categories of Dhamma.
How so in terms of the Piṭakas? For the Piṭakas are threefold:
the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, and the Sutta Piṭaka. Among these, what is the Vinaya Piṭaka?
The Pārājika-khaṇḍa, the Pācittiya-khaṇḍa, the Mahāvagga-khaṇḍa, the Cullavagga-khaṇḍa, and the Parivāra-khaṇḍa—these sections are called the Vinaya Piṭaka.
What is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka? The Dhammasaṅgaṇī treatise, the Vibhaṅga treatise, the Dhātukathā treatise, [the Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, and Paṭṭhāna].
The *Puggalapaññatti-pakaraṇa*, the *Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa*, the *Yamaka-pakaraṇa*, and the *Paṭṭhāna-pakaraṇa*.
These seven treatises are called the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. What is the Suttanta Piṭaka?
The remainder of the Buddha’s word, beginning with the Sīlakkhandha-vagga, is called the Suttanta Piṭaka.
How is it according to collection (*nikāya*)? There are five kinds of collections: the *Dīghanikāya*, the *Majjhimanikāya*, the *Saṃyuttanikāya*, the *Aṅguttaranikāya*, and the *Khuddakanikāya*.

In that regard, what is the *Dīghanikāya*? The *Sīlakkhandhavagga*, the *Mahāvagga*, and the *Pāṭikavagga*—these three sections (*vagga*) are called the *Dīghanikāya*. Within these three sections, there are thirty-four chapters (*varga*). [Thirty-four indeed...]
The discourses beginning with the Sīlakkhandha-vagga and others—those to whom these belong constitute what is called the Dīgha Nikāya.
What is the Majjhima Nikāya? The Mūla-paṇṇāsa, the Majjhima-paṇṇāsa, and the Upari-paṇṇāsa:
these three fifties (paṇṇāsas) are called the Majjhima Nikāya. Within these three fifties, there are one hundred and fifty-two discourses (diyaḍḍhasata-suttantā).
The Majjhima Nikāya, which consists of two suttas for each [discourse], begins with the Mūlapaṇṇāsa and so forth.

What is the Saṃyutta Nikāya? The Sagāthāvagga, the Nidānavagga, the Khandhakavagga, the Saḷāyatanavagga, and the Mahāvagga—these five divisions are called the Saṃyutta Nikāya. Within these five divisions, there are seven thousand six hundred and sixty-two suttas.
[There are] sixty-two, seven hundred, and seven thousand suttas. He who possesses these suttas—the Sagāthāvagga and the rest—should be known by the wise as the Saṃyutta Nikāya.
What is the Aṅguttara Nikāya? It consists of the Ekanipāta, Dukanipāta, Tikanipāta, Catukkanipāta, and Pañcakanipāta.
The Section of Six, the Section of Seven, the Section of Eight, the Section of Nine, the Section of Ten, and the Section of Eleven—these eleven sections are called the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
Within these eleven sections, there are nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven suttas.
[Nine thousand suttas, and just five hundred more, plus fifty-seven; such are the suttas of which it consists.]
[The Aṅguttara Nikāya consists of the Ekaka-nipāta and so forth.

What is the Khuddaka Nikāya? It is the Khuddakapāṭha, the Dhammapada, the Udāna, the Itivuttaka, the Suttanipāta, the Vimānavatthu, the Petavatthu, the Theragāthā, the Therīgāthā, the Jātaka, the Mahāniddesa, and the Paṭisambhidāmagga.
The Apadāna, the Buddhavaṃsa, the Cariyāpiṭaka, the Vinayapiṭaka, and the Abhidhammapiṭaka.
Within these seventeen texts, there are many thousands of suttas. [Many thousands of suttas have been pointed out by the Great Sage in these five Nikāyas, known as the Khuddaka.]

How does it become ninefold according to its constituent parts? It is ninefold by way of division: *sutta*, *geyya*, *veyyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, *itivuttaka*, *jātaka*, *abbhutadhamma*, and *vedalla*.
Among these, there are the *ubhatovibhaṅga*, the *niddesa*, the *khandhaka*, and the *parivāra*; as well as in the *Suttanipāta*, the *Maṅgalasutta*, the *Ratanasutta*, and the *Tuvaṭṭakasutta*.
Furthermore, any other word of the Tathāgata known by the name *sutta* should be understood as *sutta*. Everything that contains verses (*sagāthaka*) should be understood as *geyya*.

The entire *Sagāthakavagga* within the *Saṃyuttanikāya*, the entire *Abhidhammapiṭaka*, and whatever word of the Buddha is without verses (*nigāthaka*) and not included among the other eight factors (*aṅga*), that is *veyyākaraṇa*.
It should be understood that the *Dhammapada*, the *Theragāthā*, the *Therīgāthā*, and the pure verses not titled as individual suttas within the *Suttanipāta* are to be known as "Gāthā.
It should be understood that the eighty-two discourses (*suttanta*) beginning with the *Udāna*, which consist of verses imbued with joy and knowledge, are to be known as "Udāna.
Furthermore, the one hundred and ten discourses occurring in the manner beginning with "Thus it was said by the Blessed One" are to be known as "Itivuttaka."
They should be known. The *Apaṇṇaka-jātaka* and others, numbering fifty and so forth—these five hundred birth stories (*jātaka*) should be known as "Birth Stories.

Monks, there are four wonderful and marvelous qualities; all discourses (*suttanta*) proceeding in the manner of the *Ānanda-sutta* and others, connected with wonderful and marvelous qualities, should be known as "Marvelous Qualities.

As for the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma that are difficult to understand, if those eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma...
I shall speak in detail, but it will become too prolix. Therefore, I shall speak by way of method: one subject is one aggregate of Dhamma;
one introduction is one aggregate of Dhamma; one question asked is one aggregate of Dhamma;
one answer to a question is one aggregate of Dhamma. By what [means] are there eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma?
They have been spoken; where were they spoken? When were they spoken? With reference to whom were they spoken?
For what purpose were they spoken? By whom were they preserved? By whom were they brought down? For what purpose should they be mastered? Herein, this is the answer: By whom were they spoken?
They were spoken by Buddhas and those following the Buddhas. Where were they spoken? Among gods and among humans.
And they have been spoken. When were they spoken? They were spoken both during the time of the Blessed One’s life and in the later period.
With reference to whom were they spoken? They were spoken with reference to those to be trained, such as the group of five disciples and others.
For what purpose were they spoken? So that, having understood both the blameworthy and the blameless, one might abandon the blameworthy and practice the blameless.
Ending in Nibbāna. To attain the welfare pertaining to the present life and the future life. By whom were they preserved?
They were preserved by those who had realized [the truth] and by their disciples and grand-disciples. By whom were they brought forth? They were brought forth through the succession of teachers.
For what purpose should they be mastered? Having known what is blameworthy and what is blameless, [one should abandon the blameworthy].
Having abandoned what is blameworthy and practiced for the sake of the welfare pertaining to the present life and the future life, which culminates in Nibbāna—
in order to attain that very thing, these [teachings] culminating in Nibbāna and pertaining to the welfare of the present and future lives serve as the means.
Therefore, one should diligently master, retain, preserve, recite, and rehearse them therein.
[Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Lamp of the Three Piṭakas," in the *Cullaganthavaṃsa*.
2. Chapter on the Teachers who Composed the Texts Furthermore, there are teachers.
There are ancient teachers (*porāṇācariya*), there are teachers of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*), and there are teachers who composed the texts (*ganthakārakācariya*).
There are three types of teachers according to their names. Who are the ancient teachers (*porāṇācariyā*)?
At the first council, five hundred *khīṇāsavas* performed the work of establishing the names, meanings, intentions, and word-definitions of the five Nikāyas, as well as all other remaining tasks.
At the second council, seven hundred *khīṇāsavas* performed those same tasks concerning the words, meanings, and so forth.
They performed it again. At the Third Council, approximately one thousand *khīṇāsavas* performed once more those same tasks, such as establishing the phonology and meaning of the words.
Thus, excluding Mahākaccāyana, the remaining two thousand two hundred *khīṇāsavas* are known as the "Ancient Teachers" (*porāṇācariyā*).
Those who are the Ancient Teachers are themselves known as the "Commentarial Teachers" (*aṭṭhakathācariyā*). Who, then, are the "Text-Composing Teachers" (*ganthakārakācariyā*)?
The teachers known as the authors of treatises are the many teachers who are the Great Commentators (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathika*). What are the three types of names of teachers?
The teacher Mahākaccāyana has three names. What are the treatises composed by Mahākaccāyana?
They are the *Kaccāyana* treatise, the *Mahānirutti* treatise, the *Cullanirutti* treatise, the *Yamaka* treatise, the *Netti* treatise, and the *Peṭakopadesa* treatise.
These six books were composed by Mahākaccāyana. Which books were composed by various teachers?
The teacher Mahāpaccariya composed the book named Mahāpaccarī. The teacher Mahākurundiya composed the book named Kurundi.
A certain teacher composed a commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on the Mahāpaccarī book. A certain teacher [composed one] on the Kurundi...
He composed a commentary on the *Ganthadhātu*. The master named Buddhaghosa, known as Mahābuddhaghosa, [wrote] the *Visuddhimagga*;
the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya* called the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*; the commentary on the *Majjhimanikāya* called the *Papañcasūdanī*;
the commentary on the *Saṃyuttanikāya* called the *Sāratthappakāsinī*; and the *Manorathapūraṇī* on the *Aṅguttaranikāya*.
The commentary named *Aṭṭhasālinī*; the commentary on the five Vinaya texts named *Samantapāsādikā*;
the commentary on the seven Abhidhamma texts named *Paramatthadīpanī*; the commentary on the *Mātikā* known as the *Pātimokkha*, named *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*;
the commentary on the *Visuddhimagga*; the commentary on the *Dhammapada*; and the commentary on the *Jātaka*.
He composed these thirteen texts: the *Aṭṭhakathā* on the *Khuddakapāṭha*, the *Aṭṭhakathā* on the *Suttanipāta*, and the *Aṭṭhakathā* on the *Apadāna*.
The teacher named Buddhadata composed these four: the *Vinayavinicchaya*, the *Uttaravinicchaya*, the *Abhidhammāvatāra*, and the *Aṭṭhakathā* on the *Buddhavaṃsa* titled *Madhuratthavilāsinī*.
He composed [commentaries] on the texts. The teacher named Ānanda composed a sub-commentary (ṭīkā) called the Mūṭīka for the commentary on the seven Abhidhamma books.

The teacher Dhammapāla [composed] the Nettippakaraṇa-ṭīkā, the Itivuttaka-ṭīkā, the Udāna-ṭīkā, the Cariyāpiṭaka-ṭīkā, the Theragāthā-ṭīkā, the Therīgāthā-ṭīkā, and [the commentary] on the Vimānavatthu...
The commentary named *Vimalavilāsinī*; the commentary on the *Petavatthu* named *Vimalavilāsinī*; the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Visuddhimagga* named *Paramatthamañjūsā*;

He composed two treatises. A certain teacher composed the *Navaṭīkā* through reflection on the distinctions of word-meanings.

One minister composed three types of treatises: a commentary on the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Gaṇṭhipakaraṇa* and the *Daṇḍippakaraṇa* in the Māgadhī language, and a commentary on the work composed in the Sakaṭa dialect for the people of Koladdha. [This was done by] the Dhammasenāpati.
The teacher named Nāmācariya composed three treatises: the *Kārika*, the *Etimāsapadīpanī*, and the *Manohara*.
Another teacher composed a commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Kārika*. Another teacher composed a commentary on the *Etimāsapadīpikā*.
Another teacher composed a treatise named *Saddabindu*. The teacher named Saddhammaguru [composed] the *Saddavuttippakāsaka*.
...composed the *Nāma-pakaraṇa*. The teacher named Sāriputta composed a commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the work that elucidates the usage of words.
Another teacher composed two types of works: the treatise named *Kaccāyanasāra* and its commentary (*ṭīkā*).
The teacher named Navo Medhaṅkara composed the treatise named *Lokadīpakasāra*. [Aggapaṇḍita...]
The teacher Nāmācariya composed the treatise titled *Lokuppatti*. The teacher Cīvara composed a commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Jaṅghadāsaka*.

These eight works—the *Mātikatthadīpanī*, the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgahavaṇṇanā*, the sub-commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on the *Sīmālaṅkāra*, the sub-commentary on the *Vinayasamuṭṭhānadīpanī*, the *Gaṇṭhisāra*, the method of calculation for the *Paṭṭhāna*, the *Suttaniddesa*, and the *Pātimokkha*—are his works.
The teacher Saddhammajotipāla composed the *Gaṇṭhipada*. The teacher named Vimalabuddhi composed the treatise called the *Abhidhammapaññāsaṭṭhāna*.

The junior teacher named Vimalabuddhi composed the *Saddasāratthajālinī*, the commentary on the *Saddasāratthajālinī*, the commentary on the *Vuttodaya*, and the sub-commentary on the *Paramatthamañjūsā*—the commentary on the *Abhidhammasaṅgaha*—known as the *Dasagaṇṭhivaṇṇanā*.
He composed these six works: the *Māgadhabhāsāvidagga*, the *Mukhamaṇḍana-ṭīkā*, and so forth. Another teacher composed a new sub-commentary (*anuṭīkā*) on the commentary to the *Pañcapakaraṇa*.
The teacher named Ariyavaṃsa composed a new sub-commentary on the commentary to the *Abhidhammasaṅgaha*, titled the *Paramatthamaṇisāramañjūsā*.
[There are also] a commentary on the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*, a commentary on the *Peṭakopadesa*, and a commentary on the *Catubhāṇavāra*...
The Aṭṭhakathā, the Mahāsārapakāsanī, the Mahādīpanī, the Sāratthadīpanī-gaṇṭhipakaraṇa,
the Hatthasāra, the Bhummasaṅgaha, the Bhummaniddesa, the Dasavatthukāyavirati-ṭīkā, the Jotanā-nirutti, the Vibhattikathā, the Kaccāyanavivaraṇā,
the Saddhammamālinī, the Pañcagativannaṇā, the Bālacittapabodhana, and [the commentary] on the Dhammacakkasutta.
The *Navaṭṭhakathā* and the commentary on the *Dantadhātupakaraṇa*— these twenty works were composed by various teachers;
furthermore, there are other treatises,
such as the *Saddhammapāyana* and the commentary on the *Bālappabodhanapakaraṇa*, as well as the *Jinālaṅkārapakaraṇa*.
The *Navaṭīkā*, the *Liṅgatthavivaraṇa*, the *Liṅgavinicchaya*; the *Pātimokkhavivaraṇa*,
the *Paramatthakathāvivaraṇa*, the *Samantapāsādikāvivaraṇa*, the *Catubhāṇavāraṭṭhakathāvivaraṇa*, the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgahavivaraṇa*,
the *Saccasaṅkhepavivaraṇa*, the *Saddatthabhedacintāvivaraṇa*, the *Saddavuttivivaraṇa*, and the *Kaccāyanasāravivaraṇa*.
The *Vivaraṇa* commentary on the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*; the *Vivaraṇa* on the *Mahāvessantara-jātaka*; the *Sakkābhimata*;
the *Navaṭṭhakathā* on the *Mahāvessantara-jātaka*; the *Paṭhamasambodhi*; the *Lokanetti*; the *Milindapañhā-vaṇṇanā*, which is the introduction to the teacher Buddhaghosa;
the *Caturārakkhā*; the *Aṭṭhakathā* on the *Caturārakkhā*; and [the commentary] on the *Saddavutti-pakaraṇa*.
The *Navaṭīkā*, and thus twenty-five treatises of such proportions were composed by scholars in various places such as the island of Laṅkā;
furthermore, there are the *Sambuddhagāthā*, the verses named *Naradeva*, the verses beginning with "Dātave cīratti," the twenty verses of exhortation (*ovāda*),
the *Dānasattari*, the *Sīlasattari*, the *Sappādānavaṇṇanā*, and the verses for the infinite salutation to the Buddhas.
Furthermore, the twenty-eight verses of homage to the Buddhas, the verses of homage to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present,

the eighty verses of homage to the great disciples, and the description of the nine qualities of the Buddha— these verses beginning with the homage to the Buddha were composed by wise men in various places such as the island of Laṅkā.
[Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Teacher Dīpaka," in the Cullaganthavaṃsa.]

3. The Delimitation of the Teachers' Birthplaces. Among the teachers, there are those who are teachers from Jambudīpa and those who are teachers from Laṅkādīpa. Who are the teachers from Jambudīpa? Who are the teachers from Laṅkādīpa?
Mahākaccāyana is a teacher from Jambudīpa; he was in Ujjenī in the kingdom of Avantī.

Having served as the royal chaplain to the king named Candapajjota in the city, and having seen the peril in sensual pleasures, he abandoned the household life and went forth into the teaching of the Teacher.

He composed the treatises of the type mentioned above. These include: the Master of the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathācariya) from Jambudīpa, the Master of the Mahāpaccarī, the Master of the Mahākuṇḍī, and two other masters.

And there were the Bhūvācariyas. Those known as the Laṅkādīpikācariyas, it is said, existed during the time of the master Buddhaghosa, who was a Bhūvācariya. Master Mahābuddhaghosa was from Jambudīpa.
He, it is said, was the son of a brahmin named Kesi, the royal chaplain, in the village of Ghosaka in the kingdom of Magadha; having gone forth in the teaching of the Teacher, he [went] to Laṅkādīpa.
He composed the treatises of the type described below.

[These include: Ācariya Buddhadatta, Ācariya Ānanda, Ācariya Dhammapāla, the two Bubbācariyas, Ācariya Mahāvajirabuddha, Ācariya Cullavajirabuddha, Ācariya Dīpaṅkara known as Vimalabuddha, and Ācariya Culladīpaṅkara.
The teacher Culladhammapāla, the teacher Kassapa— these eleven teachers from Jambudīpa composed the aforementioned types of treatises.
The teacher Mahānāma, the teacher Aññatara, the teacher Cullamahānāma, the teacher Upasena, the teacher Moggalāna,
the teacher Saṅgharakkhita, the teacher Vuttodayakāra, the teacher Dhammasiri, and another...

The two teachers: the teacher Anuruddha, the teacher Khema, the teacher Sāriputta, the teacher Buddhanaṅga, the teacher Culla-Moggallāna, the teacher Vācissara, the teacher Sumaṅgala, the teacher Buddhapiya, the teacher Dhammakitti, the teacher Medhaṅkara,
the teacher Buddharakkhita, the teacher Upatissa, and another twenty teachers, including the teacher Saddhammasiri.
The teacher Devācariya, the teacher Cullabuddhaghosa, the teacher Sāriputta, and the teacher Raṭṭhapāla—
these two groups of fifty teachers are known as the teachers of Laṅkādīpa. The teacher Subhūtacanda, the teacher Aggavaṃsa,
the new teacher Vajirabuddhi, the teacher Guṇasāgara, the teacher Abhaya, the teacher Ñāṇasāgara, two other teachers, and the teacher Uttama.
A certain teacher, a certain great minister, the teacher Dhammasenāpati, three other teachers, the teacher Saddhammaguru,
the teacher Sāriputta, another single teacher, the teacher Medhaṅkara, the teacher Aggapaṇḍita, the teacher Cīvara,
the teacher Saddhammajotipāla, and the teacher Vimalabuddhi— these are the twenty-three teachers.
The Jambudīpika [teacher] composed the aforementioned treatises in the city of Arimaddana, known as Pukāma.
The teacher Navovimalabuddha, a native of Jambudīpa, composed the aforementioned treatises in the city of Paṃya.
These two teachers—the teacher Aññatara and the teacher Ariyavaṃsa—were both natives of Jambudīpa who [composed] the aforementioned treatises.
In the city of Atavi, certain teachers from Jambudīpa belonging to the Vīsativagga school made some additions to the texts of the kind previously mentioned in the house of Purādi.
[Thus ends the third chapter in the Cullaganthavaṃsa, titled "The Indicator of the Places Where the Teachers Were Born."]
4. The Chapter on the Teachers of the Invitation As for the texts, they may have been composed by teachers through invitation, or they may have been composed by teachers without invitation.
Which texts were composed through invitation, and which were composed without invitation? The text of Mahākaccāyana and the text of the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*).
The Mahāpaccarī commentary, the Mahākuṇḍalī commentary, the commentary on the Mahāpaccarī,
and the commentary on the Mahākuṇḍalī— these six commentaries were composed by his own intellect for the purpose of upholding the Dispensation and for the stability of the True Dhamma.
Ka. *Buddhaghosācariya-ganthadīpanā*:
Among the works of the Master Buddhaghosa, the *Visuddhimagga* was composed by the Master Buddhaghosa at the request of the Elder Saṅghapāla.
The commentary on the *Dīghanikāya* was [composed] by the Elder named Dāṭhā.
The commentary on the *Majjhimanikāya* was composed by the teacher Buddhaghosa at the request of the elder named Buddhamitta.
The commentary on the *Saṃyuttanikāya* was composed by the teacher Buddhaghosa at the request of the elder named Jotipāla. The commentary on the *Aṅguttaranikāya*...
The work called *Bhaddantā* was composed by the teacher Buddhaghosa at the request of the Elder [Buddhadatta], the co-resident (sahājīvaka), and the lay follower (upāsaka).
The commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) called *Samantapāsādikā* was composed by the teacher Buddhaghosa at the request of the Elder named Buddhasīri.
The commentary on the seven Abhidhamma texts was composed by the bhikkhu Cullabuddhaghosa.
The commentary on the *Dhammapada* was composed by the teacher Buddhaghosa at the request of the elder named Kumārakassapa.
The commentary on the *Jātaka* was composed by the teacher Buddhaghosa at the request of three elders known as Atthadassī, Buddhamitta, and Buddhapiyadeva.
The *Kato*: the commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha* was composed by the teacher Buddhaghosa according to his own judgment.

The commentary on the *Suttanipāta* was composed by the teacher Buddhaghosa at the request of five elders who were learned in the five Nikāyas. The commentary on the *Apadāna* was composed by the teacher Buddhaghosa when he had been entreated by those same five elders.
The *Ganthadīpanā* by the teacher Buddhaghosa is completed.
Section Kha: The *Ganthadīpanā* by the teacher Buddhadatta.
Furthermore, among the works of the teacher Buddhatta, the *Vinayavinicchayagrantha* was [composed] by his own pupil, Buddhasīha.
The *Uttaravinicchaya* treatise was composed by the teacher Buddhadatta at the request of the elder named Saṅghapāla.
The treatise called the *Abhidhammāvatāra* was composed by the teacher Buddhadatta at the request of his own disciple, the elder Sumati. [Also] the commentary on the *Buddhavaṃsa*.
This work was composed by the teacher Buddhadatta at the request of the elder named Buddhasiha.
The *Ganthadīpanā* on the teacher Buddhadatta’s work is finished.
The commentary on the *Abhidhammakathā*, titled the *Mūlaṭīkā*, was composed by the teacher Ānanda at the request of the elder named Buddhamitta.
The *Nettipakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*, titled *Ganthadīpanā*, was composed by the teacher Dhammapāla at the request of the elder named Dhammarakkhita.
Also [included are] the *Itivuttaka-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā*. The *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā*...
The *Gantho*, the commentary on the *Theragāthā*, the commentary on the *Therīgāthā*, the commentary on the *Vimānavatthu*,
and the commentary on the *Petavatthu*— these seven works were composed by the teacher Dhammapāla according to his own understanding.
The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Visuddhimagga* was composed by the teacher Dhammapāla at the request of the elder named Dāṭha.
The following five works were composed by the teacher Dhammapāla according to his own understanding: a commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the four commentaries beginning with the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*;
a sub-commentary (*anuṭīkā*) on the *Abhidhamma-aṭṭhakathā*; a commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Nettipakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*;
a commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Buddhavaṃsa-aṭṭhakathā*; and a commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*.
The *Dhammapālācariya-ganthadīpanā* is completed.
The work titled *Cullaniruttiṭīkā*, known as the *Niruttimañjūsā*, and the work titled *Mahāniruttisaṅkhepa* were composed by me according to my own understanding from the works of former teachers.
The work titled *Vinayagaṇṭhi*, concerning the five sections of the Vinaya, was composed by me according to my own understanding by the teacher Mahāvajirabuddhi.
The work known as *Nyāsa*, titled *Mukhamattadīpanī*, was composed by the teacher Vimalabuddhi according to his own judgment.
The work titled *Atthabyākhyāna* was composed by the teacher Cullavajirabuddhi according to his own judgment.
Furthermore, the *Rūpasiddhi* and its commentary (*Ṭīkā*), as well as the *Sabbapañcasutta*, were composed by the teacher Dīpaṅkara according to his own judgment.
The *Saccasaṅkhepa* (Compendium of Truths), a treatise composed by his own teacher Culla-Dhammapāla according to his own wisdom;

the *Mohacchedanī* (Destroyer of Delusion) and *Vimaticchedanī* (Destroyer of Doubt) treatises; the *Dasabuddhavaṃsa* (Lineage of Ten Buddhas) and the *Anāgatavaṃsa* (Chronicle of Future Buddhas)—these were composed by his own teacher Kassapa according to his own wisdom.
The commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* was composed by the teacher Mahānāma at the request of the lay follower Mahānāma.

The *Kato*, the *Dīpavaṃsa*, the *Thūpavaṃsa*, the *Bodhivaṃsa*, the *Cullavaṃsa*, and the *Porāṇavaṃsa*—these six texts were composed separately by the teacher Mahānāma according to his own judgment.
The new *Mahāvaṃsa* text was composed by the teacher Culla-Mahānāma according to his own judgment.
The commentary on the *Mahāniddesa* named *Saddhammapajjotikā*.
The *Gantho* was composed by the Elder Thera Upasena at the request of the King. The *Moggalānabyākaraṇa* was composed by the teacher Moggalāna according to his own judgment.
The treatise named *Subodhālaṅkāra* was composed by the teacher Saṅgharakkhita according to his own judgment.
The *Vuttodaya* treatise was composed by the teacher who authored the *Vuttodaya* according to his own judgment. The [treatise] named *Khuddasikkhā*...
The *Gantho* was composed by Dhammasirī Ācariya according to his own judgment.
Both the *Porāṇakhuddasikkhā-ṭīkā* and the *Mūlasikkhā* were composed by certain other two teachers according to their own judgment.
The treatise named *Paramatthavinicchaya* was [composed] by the teacher Anuruddha at the request of the Elder Saṅgharakkhita.
The *Kato*: a treatise titled *Nāmarūpa-pariccheda* composed by the teacher Anuruddha according to his own insight.
The treatise titled *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha* was composed by the teacher Anuruddha at the request of the lay devotee named Nāma.

The treatise titled *Khema* was composed by the teacher Khema according to his own insight. The treatise titled *Sāratthadīpanī* is a sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) to the Vinaya.
The *Vinayasaṅgaha*, its commentary (*ṭīkā*) treatise, and the new commentary treatise on the *Aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathā*—
these four treatises were composed by the teacher Sāriputta at the request of the sovereign King Parakkamabāhu of the island of Laṅkā.
Furthermore, the commentary treatise on the *Sakaṭasaddasattha-pañcikā* was composed by the teacher Sāriputta according to his own wisdom.
The *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* commentary, titled *Vinayatthamañjūsā*, was composed by the teacher Buddhanāga at the request of the thera named Sumedha.
The work titled *Abhidhānappadīpikā* was composed by the teacher Cūḷamoggallāna through his own intelligence.
Furthermore, there are these two works: the commentary on the *Subodhālaṅkāra* titled *Mahāsāmi*, and the *Vuttodayavivaraṇa*.
The *Khuddasikkhā-ṭīkā* named *Sumaṅgalappasādani*, a new work composed by Navācissara at the request of Sumaṅgala,
was written by Vācissara according to his own judgment. Furthermore, these three works— the *Sambandhacintā-ṭīkā Bālāvatāra* and the *Moggallānabyākaraṇa-ṭīkā*—
were composed by three elders known as Sumaṅgala, Buddhamitta, and Mahākassapa.
And [this work] was composed by Vācissara at the request of the lay follower named Dhammakitti and the merchant lay follower who was his brother.

These seven [works] are: the *Nāmarūpaparicchedavibhāga*, the *Saddatthapadārūpavibhāvana*, the commentary on the *Khemapakaraṇa*, the *Sīmālaṅkāra*, the commentary on the *Mūlasikkhā*, the *Rūpavibhāga*, and the *Paccayasaṅgaha*.
The *Ganthā* was composed by Vācissara according to his own judgment.
The commentary on the *Saccasaṅkhepa*, known as the *Ganthā*, was composed by the Elder named Sāriputta at the request of Vācissara.

The two works known as the commentary on the *Abhidhammāvatāra* and the commentary on the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha* were composed by the teacher Sumaṅgala according to his own judgment. [Also] the work named *Sāratthasaṅgaha*.

The treatise titled *Dantadhātuvannanā* (A Description of the Tooth Relic), a composition made by his own intellect by Buddhapiya at the request of the general of the King who was the Lord of the Island of Laṅkā, was composed by the teacher named Dhammakitti.
The treatise titled *Jinacarita* (The Life of the Victor) was composed by his own intellect by the teacher Medhaṅkara. [And] the *Jinālaṅkāra*... of the *Jinālaṅkāra*.
The *Ṭīkā* was composed by the teacher Buddharakkhita according to his own judgment.
The commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on the *Anāgatavaṃsa*, titled *Amatadharo*, was composed by the teacher Upatissa according to his own judgment. [Also included are:
the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-ṭīkā*, the *Līnatthappakāsinī*, the *Nisandeho*, the *Dhammānusāraṇī*, the *Ñeyyasantati*, the *Ṭīkā* on the *Ñeyyasantati*, the *Sumatāvatāro*, and the *Lokapaññatti*.
The *Pakaraṇa*, the *Tathāgatuppatti-pakaraṇa*, the *Nalāṭadhātu-vaṇṇanā*, the *Sīhaḷavatthu*,
the *Dhammadīpaka-paṭipatti-saṅgaha*, the *Visuddhimagga-gaṇṭhi*, the *Abhidhamma-gaṇṭhi*, the *Netti-pakaraṇa-gaṇṭhi*,
the *Visuddhimaggacūḷa-navatīkā*, the *Sotabbamālinī*, the *Pasādajananī*, the *Okassaloka*, and [the commentary] on the *Subodhālaṅkāra*.
And the *Navaṭīkā*—these twenty works were composed by twenty teachers, each according to his own intelligence.
The treatise named *Saddatthabhedacintā* was composed by the teacher named Saddhammasiri according to his own intelligence.
The treatise named *Sumanakūṭavaṇṇanā* was [composed] by the Elder Vācissara at the request of the Elder Rāhula.
The *Sotatthaki*—the treatise named *Mahānidāna*—was composed by the teacher Cullabuddhaghosa according to his own judgment.
The treatise named *Madhurasaṅgaha* was composed by the teacher Raṭṭhapāla according to his own judgment.
The treatise named *Liṅgatthavivaraṇa* was composed by the teacher Subhūtacanda according to his own judgment. The *Saddanīti* treatise [was composed] by himself...
The *Nyāsapakaraṇa-mahāṭīkā* was composed by the teacher Vajirabuddhi according to his own understanding.
The *Mukhamattasāra* was composed by the teacher Guṇasāgara according to his own understanding.
The commentary on the *Mukhamattasāra*, requested by the Elder Saṅgha, the preceptor of King Dhammarāja, who was endowed with learning, [was composed] by [the author] named Sutasampanna.
The *Mahāṭīkā* on the *Saddatthabhedacintā* was composed by the teacher Abhaya according to his own judgment.
The treatise named *Liṅgatthavivaraṇappakāsaka* was composed by the teacher Ñāṇasāgara according to his own judgment.
Furthermore, two types of treatises—the *Ṭīkā* on the *Guḷhattha* and the *Bālappabodhana*—were composed by a certain other teacher according to his own judgment.
The *Saddatthabhedacintā-ṭīkā* was composed by a certain teacher according to his own judgment.
The commentary on the *Bālāvatāra* and the commentary on the *Liṅgatthavivaraṇa* were composed by a preeminent teacher according to his own judgment.
Nine commentaries on the *Saddatthabhedacintā* were composed by a certain teacher according to his own judgment. [There is also] a commentary on the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* and the *Daṇḍīpakaraṇa*.
There are two types of commentaries (*ṭīkā*): those composed according to one's own judgment, and that composed by a certain minister of King Sīhasūra named Magaghabhūta.
The *Koladdhajanasaṭīkā* was composed by that same great minister at the request of the Elder named Pāsādika.
The treatise known as the *Kārikā* was composed by the teacher Dhammasenāpati at the request of a monk named Ñāṇagambhīra.

The work called *Etimāsamidīpanī* (or *Etimāsamidīpikā*), which is captivating and composed by that very teacher, the General of the Dhamma (*Dhammasenāpati*), has been made according to his own judgment.
A commentary on the *Kārikā* was composed according to his own judgment by a certain other teacher.
A commentary on the *Etimāsamidīpikā* was composed according to his own judgment by a certain other teacher.
The *Saddabindu-pakaraṇa* was composed by a certain teacher, a preceptor of the Dhammarāja, according to his own understanding.
The treatise named *Saddavuttippakāsaka* was composed by a teacher named Saddhammaguru at the request of a certain bhikkhu.
A commentary on the *Saddavuttippakāsaka* was composed by the teacher Sāriputta according to his own understanding.
The *Kaccāyana-sāra* and its commentary, the *Kaccāyana-sāra-ṭīkā*, are two treatises composed by a certain teacher through his own intelligence.
The treatise named *Lokadīpaka-sāra* was composed by the teacher Navamēdhankara through his own intelligence.
The *Lokuppatti-pakaraṇa* was composed by the teacher Aggapandita through his own intelligence. [There is also] the *Jaṅghadāsaka-ṭīkā*.
The *Bhūta-magadha-ṭīkā* was composed by his own teacher, Cīvarācariya, according to his own judgment.

The *Mātikatthadīpanī*, the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha-vaṇṇanā*, the *Sīmālaṅkāra-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Gaṇṭhisāra*, and the *Paṭṭhānagaṇanānaya*—these five treatises were composed by his own teacher, Saddhammajotipāla, according to his own judgment. The *Saṅkhepavaṇṇanā* was composed by the lord of Jambudīpa named Parakkamabāhu.
The *Saddhammajotipāla-ācariya* composed this at the request of the King.
The *Kaccāyana-sutta-niddesa* was composed by the teacher Saddhammajotipāla at the request of his own pupil, the Elder Dhammacārin.
The treatise named *Vinayasamuṭṭhāna-dīpanī* was composed by the teacher Saddhammajotipāla at the request of his own preceptor, the Saṅghatthera.
The *Sattappakaraṇāni* were composed by him in the city of Pukkamana. The *Saṅkhepavaṇṇanā* was composed on the island of Laṅkā.
The treatise named *Abhidhammapannarasaṭṭhānavaṇṇanā* was composed by the teacher Vimalabuddha, a contemporary, according to his own wisdom.
The treatise named *Saddasāratthajālinī* was composed by the teacher Vimalabuddha, a contemporary, according to his own wisdom.
The *Saddasāratthajālinī-Ṭīkā*, composed by that same newly arisen teacher Vimalabuddhi at the request of the Saṅgharāja, who was the royal preceptor in the city of Paṃyanagara; the *Vuttodaya-Ṭīkā*;
the sub-commentary (*anuṭīkā*) named *Paramatthamañjūsā* on the *Abhidhammasaṅgaha-Ṭīkā*; the treatise named *Dasagaṇṭhivaṇṇanā*; and the commentary on the *Magadhabhūtavidaggamukhamaṇḍanī*.
These four treatises were composed by that very same teacher Vimalabuddhi according to his own judgment and with his own new [insight].
A new sub-commentary (*anuṭīkā*) to the commentary on the *Pañcapakaraṇa* was composed by a certain teacher according to his own judgment.
A new commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Abhidhammasaṅgaha* was composed by a certain teacher according to his own judgment. [The *Maṇi*] commentary on the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*...
The *Mañjūsā*—also known as the *Maṇisāramañjūsā*—is a new sub-commentary composed by the teacher Ariyavaṃsa according to his own judgment.
A commentary on the *Peṭakopadesa* was composed by the teacher named Udumbara according to his own judgment in the city of Pukkāma.
[There are also] the commentary on the *Catubhāṇavāra*, the *Mahāsārapakāsini*, the *Mahādīpanī*, the *Sāratthadīpanī*, the *Gatipakaraṇa*, and the *Hatthāsāra*.
The *Bhummasaṅgaha*, the *Bhummaniddesa*, the commentary on the ten bases of abstention from bodily misconduct, the *Codanānirutti*, the *Vibhattikathā*,
the *Saddhammamālinī*, the *Pañcagativaṇṇanā*, the *Bālacittapabodhanaṃ*, the ninefold commentary on the *Dhammacakkasutta*, the commentary on the *Dantadhātupakaraṇa*—
namely the *Saddhammopāyana* and the *Bālappabodhanaṭīkā*— and [the commentary] on the *Jinālaṅkāra*.
The *Navaṭīkā*, the *Liṅgatthavivaraṇa*, the *Liṅgatthavinicchaya*, the *Pātimokkhavivaraṇa*, the *Paramatthakathāvivaraṇa*, the *Samantapāsādikāvivaraṇa*,
the *Catubhāṇavāra-aṭṭhakathāvivaraṇa*, the *Abhidhammasaṅgahavivaraṇa*, the *Saccasaṅkhepavivaraṇa*,
the *Saddatthabhedacintāvivaraṇa*, the *Saddavuttivivaraṇa*, and the *Kaccāyanasāravivaraṇa*.
The Kaccāyanavivaraṇa; the Ṭīkāvivaraṇa on the Abhidhammasaṅgaha; the Vivaraṇa on the Mahāvessantarajātakaya; the Sakkābhimata;
the Navaṭṭhakathā on the Mahāvessantarajātakaya; the Paṭhamasambodhi; the Lokanetti; the Buddhadhosa-ācariya-nidāna;
the Vaṇṇanā on the Milindapañha; the Caturārakkhā; and the Aṭṭhakathā on the Caturārakkhā.

The *Saddavutti-pakaraṇa-ṭīkā*—these forty-three treatises were composed by me, according to my own intelligence, in various locations such as the island of Laṅkā, for the sake of the lineage of the Dispensation and the endurance of the True Dhamma.
The verses beginning with the homage to the Buddha, from "Sambuddhe gāthā" ... up to "Navahāraguṇavaṇṇanā," are these verses starting with the salutation to the Buddha. [By] myself...

In order to manifest his own qualities as a Buddha and to cause the turning of infinite wisdom for both himself and others, twenty [treatises] were composed by the wise in various places such as the island of Laṅkā.
[Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Culla-Ganthavaṃsa*, titled "The Lamp of the Teachers Who Requested [the Texts]. ]

5. The Section on Miscellaneous Matters (Pakiṇṇaka-pariccheda) I shall speak immediately thereafter of the ascription of a name, the book, and the author; as well as the writing and the act of causing it to be written.
In that regard, the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) consist of the Piṭakas, the Nikāyas, the Aṅgas, the Vaggas, the Nipātas, and so forth.
[One might ask: "By whom was this name assigned? Where was it assigned? When was it assigned? For what purpose was it assigned? To this, the following is the response: "By whom was it assigned?
It was assigned by five hundred *khīṇāsava* (those whose taints are destroyed). They recited the entire word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*), [categorizing it as]:
"This is the Piṭaka; this is the Nikāya; this is the Aṅga; this is the Vagga; this is the Nipāta," and so forth.
They assign a name. Where was it assigned? It was assigned at Rājagaha, at the foot of Mount Vebhāra, in the Dhamma-maṇḍapa. When was it assigned?
It was assigned at the time of the First Council, after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna. For what purpose was it assigned?
It was assigned for the sake of ease in terminology and for the sake of easy retention of the divisions of the Dhamma. At the time of the recitation—
Five hundred of those whose taints were exhausted [performed] the naming and categorizing of these Dhamma aggregates.
They said, "Let this be the name of this Dhamma aggregate, and let this be the name of this treatise," and they performed all the necessary tasks such as naming.

Those whose taints were exhausted [did this] because if the tasks such as naming had not been performed, it would not be well-arranged; therefore, for the sake of ease in conventional usage, they performed the naming and other tasks.
The duty has been performed; however, for the sake of the future, names and so forth have been introduced. That which has not yet arisen will not be fully manifested in its entirety.
The exposition of the names of the aggregates of Dhamma is completed.
By whom were the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma inscribed in books? When were they inscribed? For what purpose?
"Regarding the phrase 'they were inscribed': here is the answer. By whom were they inscribed?
They were inscribed by the Great Nāgas whose taints were exhausted. Where were they inscribed? They were inscribed on the island of Laṅkā. When were they inscribed?
They were inscribed during the time of King Vaṭṭagāmaṇi, the son of King Saddhātissa. For what purpose were they inscribed? For the sake of preventing the destruction of the divisions of the Dhamma."
And they were established for the endurance of the true Dhamma.
For as long as the Blessed One, our wise Sugata, remains alive,
he teaches the five Nikāyas until the attainment of Nibbāna.
All those monks were the beginning [of the lineage], sustained by mind and speech;
they all brought [the Dhamma] forth in words, being endowed with great wisdom and a hundred years of life.
After the Lord of the World had attained Parinibbāna, there would then be one hundred years.
Both the noble ones and the non-noble ones—all those who have uttered [the words]—are certainly included.
Beyond that, there are eighteen hundred and twenty years in number;
all these are indeed both ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) and noble ones (*ariya*).
Whether by mind or by speech, or indeed always as it issues forth from the voice—
such was the case for King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī, and certainly so at that time.
Both the noble and the ignoble were constantly committed to memory within the Nikāyas.
After that, the king passed away and was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
There he arose in the world of the gods, surrounded by deities;
his beloved younger brother was named Saddhātissa.
Then he obtained a kingdom and became a protector of the Buddha’s dispensation.
At that time, all the bhikkhus were constantly proficient in speech regarding the fivefold Nikāyas,
as long as the king maintained his reign.
Then, passing away from there, that king was reborn in Tusita;
while remaining in the world of the gods, he then uttered these words.
His sons also became many, having attained excellent sovereignty.
In due course, having passed away, they surely went to the world of the gods.
At that time, all those bhikkhus likewise always had the five Nikāyas committed to memory, possessing a mastery of retention.
After that, the five Nikāyas were written upon books;
at that time, all the commentaries and sub-commentaries—indeed, all the texts—were contained within books.
Whatever texts were in those books consisted of the Pāḷi, the commentaries, and the sub-commentaries.
Some were established and some were not; none of us remained unestablished.
At that time, the Nikāyas and Piṭakas were written down in books;
they say that it was at that time that the Aṭṭhakathās and other works came into being.
The rebuttal must indeed be stated by the wise:
"Faith belongs to King Tissa, the king of the island of Laṅkā.
He is the dear son of the lord of the island of Laṅkā, righteous and excellent."
Then all those whose taints were destroyed gazed into the future.
Those whose taints were destroyed saw only two individuals of dull wisdom among the worldlings;
yet all those monks were [themselves] worldlings, for worldlings were far more numerous.
Thinking, "These five Nikāyas will not remain as they have been recited from memory," those whose taints are destroyed shall commit all five in writing into books,
for the long endurance of the True Dhamma and for the merit of people.
From that time onwards, all the Nikāyas came to exist in books;
all the Aṭṭhakathās and Ṭīkās likewise became established in books.
From that time onwards, all the great assemblies, beginning with the Bhikkhus, [came to be so].
As long as they remain in books, all people see them at all times.
[The section on the illumination of committing [the teachings] to books is finished.
Whatever wise and steadfast person composes or causes to be composed a text such as a commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) and so forth, for that person there is an infinite...
There is an accumulation of merit; the fruit of that merit is infinite.

It is equal to the making of eighty-four thousand reliquaries, equal to the making of eighty-four thousand Buddha-images, equal to the planting of eighty-four thousand Bodhi trees, and equal to the building of eighty-four thousand monasteries for one who composes or causes to be composed a treasury of the Buddha’s word.
Or, whoever adorns the word of the Buddha or causes it to be adorned; whoever writes down the word of the Buddha or causes it to be written down;
whoever provides a manuscript or the materials for a manuscript, or gives or causes them to be given;
and whoever provides oil, powder, grain, or any other requisite for the purpose of preparing a manuscript—[all these are likewise].

Or if one gives or causes to be given anything for inserting into a book—such as thread, or two pieces of wood or a board for the purpose of folding the book, or any kind of cloth; or anything for binding the book, such as a string;
or anything for wrapping a bundle of books, such as a bag.
Whoever makes an ornament for a book using yellow orpiment, or red arsenic, or gold, or silver,
or has one made, for that person there is an infinite accumulation of merit and an infinite reward of merit.
It is equal to the making of eighty-four thousand cetiyas, and equal to the making of eighty-four thousand monasteries.
Being reborn in existence, having attained the quality of virtue,
he always possesses great splendor, and his lion’s roar is confident.
Endowed with long life, beauty, and strength, he becomes one who delights in the Dhamma.
In the worlds of devas and humans, he is of great influence and free from affliction.
When being reborn in existence, wise and well-concentrated,
he attains sovereignty, a retinue, and all forms of happiness.
Possessing faith and moral dread, being generous and having a stirred mind;
endowed with all limbs and members, and possessing the proper proportions of height and girth;
he who is worthy of honor everywhere in the world among all beings—[such a one is a true disciple].
A traveler between gods and humans, protected by his friends and companions,
he enjoys the prosperity of gods and humans again and again;
having attained the fruit of arahantship, he will reach Nibbāna.
The four analytical knowledges, the sixfold noble superknowledges,
and the eight excellent liberations— he shall go there in the future.
Therefore, a wise person, considering his own welfare, [should practice].
One should personally transcribe the texts and cause others to do so as well.
While the texts— including the Pāḷi, the Aṭṭhakathā, and other works such as the *Dhammamañjūsā*—
remain in manuscript form, one should write them down or cause them to be written.
Books and the materials for books, their small stūpas as well;
rags and so forth, thread, and both types of wood and fruit;
and whatever costly cloth is used for the purpose of binding the Dhamma.
One should give a cord for binding Dhamma, and whatever small bag there may be,
at this field of Dhamma with a serene mind;
and others as well one should cause to give— friends, companions, and kinsmen.
The exposition of the benefits of composing, transcribing, and causing others to transcribe books is completed.
[Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Cūlaganthavaṃsa*, titled "The Illuminator of Miscellaneous Matters.
I, who was born in Haṃsāraṭṭha, am known as Nantapañña.
Endowed with faith, virtue, and heroism, seeking the flavor of the Dhamma,
I went from there to this new city that was full of conquerors.
Searching through all the teachings, O Victor, I have arrived here after twenty years.
A monk who dissolves all phenomena does not engage in idle chatter;
having split the assembly of six years, he crushes the desires.
There is both the assembly and Nibbāna; he seeks them again and again.
"I am Vasantō, whose resort is the forest; this is the Minor Chronicle of Books (*Cūḷaganthavaṃsa*), a compendium of the Three Piṭakas, composed by Ariyasaṅghadāsaka.
Thus ends the *Cūḷaganthavaṃsa*, composed for the sake of gladness by the forest-dweller Nandapaññācariya.
The Elder renowned by the name Dhammavaṭaṃsaka has completed this treatise that was written; by that merit, may this Piṭaka be mastered and brought to completion.
May it be mastered and brought to completion for me alone, for the assembly of my disciples, and for your own disciples and grand-disciples.
The Cūḷaganthavaṃsa is finished.
